column4: The section's dictionary sense of أَمُون is a dependable camel; this ayah directly invites readers to look at camels, الْإِبِلِ, and how they were created.

The section's dependable camel, exhausted traveler, and destination town converge in animals carrying heavy loads to a far country reachable only with great hardship, تَحْمِلُ أَثْقَالَكُمْ إِلَىٰ بَلَدٍ.

The section's dictionary family for بَلَد includes a camel's side falling to earth; here sacrificial camels stand and then their sides fall, فَإِذَا وَجَبَتْ جُنُوبُهَا, before people eat and feed others.
The section's word أَحْكَم joins securing workmanship against spoilage with judgment; this ayah uses the same root for a Book whose verses were made firm, أُحْكِمَتْ آيَاتُهُ.
The section contrasts God's true creation with human fabrication; Abraham asks about worshipping what people carve, مَا تَنْحِتُونَ, making human craft the scene's concrete example.
The section says the root خ ل ق separates God's creation from human making; this neighboring ayah says God created both people and what they do, وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ.
The section's Moses-at-the-Tur scene includes fear at a transformed form; this ayah shows the staff becoming a moving serpent, the startling event answered by reassurance in the next verse.
The section's fear-to-safety meeting and return of a thing to its former state meet God's command to take the staff without fear and His promise to restore it, سَنُعِيدُهَا سِيرَتَهَا الْأُولَىٰ.
The section's well-proportioned human meets God's announcement that He will create a human from sounding clay; this verse begins the explicit formation scene.
The section's straightened body meets the completion of that creation when God has proportioned the human and breathed of His spirit, سَوَّيْتُهُ; this neighbor names the bodily act behind taqwim.
The section's best-formed human meets the repeated announcement of a human created from clay; this is a second Qur'anic telling of the formation scene.
The section's fashioned body meets the continuation in which God proportions the human and breathes of His spirit; this neighboring retelling confirms the same creation-to-form sequence.
The section's creation, return, and denial of dīn meet the question whether people thought they were created without purpose and would not be returned to God.
The section's sound deeds and uncut reward meet the lasting righteous deeds, الْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ, said to be better in reward and hope than transient wealth and children.

The section asks what can still make a person deny the Recompense after creation and return; this ayah asks whether a human thinks he will be left without purpose, أَيَحْسَبُ الْإِنسَانُ أَن يُتْرَكَ سُدًى.
The section's outwardly measured deed and inwardly sound work meet the distinction that neither meat nor blood reaches God, but piety does; this neighbor explains what the sacrifice means.

The section's bodily descent and lasting wage meet worldly life pictured as rain-grown plants that dry into windblown debris, هَشِيمًا تَذْرُوهُ الرِّيَاحُ; the next verse names what remains valuable.
The section's exhausted traveler and mortal life meet the denial that the Creator was wearied by the first creation; the verse contrasts human fatigue with God's power to create anew.
The section's fatigued traveler and return from bodily decline meet the question whether the Creator, who made heaven and earth without weariness, can revive the dead.
The section brings a well-formed human into a meeting with height and place; after the camel, this neighboring ayah asks readers to consider how heaven was raised.
The section's straight, measured forms meet the next object in the same contemplation: mountains set firmly in place; this ayah continues the camel-and-creation scene.
The section's safe town and earth-bound descent meet the final object in the contemplation, the earth spread out; this verse completes the sequence begun with the camel.

The section's reliable camel meets the Qur'anic account of livestock created for human benefit, including warmth and food; it supplies the practical setting for the carrying animals in the next verses.
The section's sturdy animal and provision meet the beauty people find in bringing livestock home and taking them out to pasture; this neighbor continues the same animal scene.
The section's travel and load-bearing animal meet horses, mules, and donkeys provided for riding and adornment; this neighbor extends the journey scene beyond camels.
The section's root ح ك م includes making something firm; this ayah distinguishes firmly established verses, مُحْكَمَاتٌ, from ambiguous ones, a textual instance of that quality.
The section links upright human form with the root ق و م and dīn; this ayah names Abraham's straight path and a correct religion, دِينًا قِيَمًا.
The section's uprightness and just judgment meet the statement that judgment belongs to God and this is the correct religion, الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ; it joins both senses of the section's root.

The section's dictionary sense of م ن ن includes a cut rope, while this ayah tells believers to hold together to God's rope, حَبْلِ اللَّهِ, and not split apart; it offers a specific image of a bond kept intact.
The section's fire encounter turns fear toward safety; at this point in the same scene the voice identifies itself as God, grounding the following command not to fear.
The section's return to the just Judge meets the declaration that God is the true King and Lord of the noble Throne; this neighbor completes the answer to the claim of purposeless creation.
The section's formed human and return through bodily stages meet creation in the womb, خَلْقًا مِّن بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ; this ayah adds the hidden stages before birth.
The section's well-formed body meets human emergence from the mothers' wombs without knowledge, then hearing, sight, and hearts given by God; the verse makes bodily capacity a provision.
